teaching_documents.title: The Sun, fusion and outward energy transfer
teaching_documents.content: The Sun is a star held together by gravity. Its core produces energy as hydrogen nuclei combine into helium. Energy moves outward through the radiative zone and then through a region where hot plasma rises and cooler plasma sinks. The visible photosphere releases radiation into space; some reaches Earth. The Sun formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust, and its structure changes over its lifetime. A model of solar energy should distinguish energy production in the core, transfer within the star and radiation traveling through space.

teaching_documents.title: Plate boundaries and changing landforms
teaching_documents.content: At spreading boundaries, plates separate and rising magma forms new oceanic crust. At some convergent boundaries, one plate descends beneath another; collisions between continents can instead thicken and raise crust. Transform boundaries involve plates sliding sideways. These different movements help explain the locations of ridges, trenches, mountains and earthquakes. Seafloor spreading transports crust away from a ridge over geological time. Repeated measurements of points on Earth, including satellite-based measurements, can track present motion. A boundary diagram represents relative movement, while a map shows where those processes occur.

teaching_documents.title: Isotopic clocks and geological evidence
teaching_documents.content: Some isotopes change into other isotopes through radioactive decay. A half-life describes the interval in which half of an initial quantity of a radioactive parent decays. Measuring parent and daughter isotopes in suitable minerals helps estimate when those minerals formed. Different isotopic systems suit different materials and timescales. Dates from igneous layers can bracket the ages of nearby sedimentary deposits, connecting numerical ages with their relative sequence. Comparing suitable dating methods strengthens an interpretation. An age measurement must be connected to the material and event actually dated.

teaching_documents.title: Water stores, transfers and human changes
source_sections: Pools: Where and how water is stored.
teaching_documents.content: Water is stored in oceans, air, ice, soil and underground. Transfers connect these stores rather than following one simple circular route. Evaporation moves liquid water into the atmosphere as vapor; condensation forms droplets; precipitation returns water to the surface. Water can flow over land or enter soil and groundwater. Solar energy supports evaporation, while gravity helps move water downward. People change pathways and storage through dams, diversions and withdrawals. A useful model labels both the stores and the transfers and recognizes that water quality affects availability.

teaching_documents.title: Air masses, fronts and weather maps
teaching_documents.content: Uneven solar heating contributes to large-scale atmospheric circulation. Air masses develop temperature and moisture characteristics related to the regions where they form. A front is a boundary between air masses: a cold front replaces warmer air with colder air, while a warm front advances warmer air. Weather maps help locate and follow these boundaries. Strong upper-atmosphere winds steer weather systems and transfer heat and moisture. Earth’s rotation deflects moving air. Interpreting a sequence of maps connects changing local conditions to moving air masses instead of treating each weather observation as isolated.
